package_info.package_versions: ctx: 0.1.2 and other recent versions after 8 years of inactivity; PHPass: 0.3.x-dev (recent commit)
package_info.why_malicious: Both packages were hijacked and modified to include code that exfiltrates sensitive environment variables, specifically targeting AWS credentials, to an external endpoint controlled by the attacker. This constitutes a supply chain attack and credential theft, as the malicious code is executed automatically upon import or class instantiation, compromising any system using the affected versions.

execution_context.trigger: constructor-time (whenever the PasswordHash class is instantiated)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: When the PasswordHash class is instantiated, the code reads AWS credentials from environment variables and sends them via an HTTP GET request to a remote Heroku endpoint controlled by the attacker.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code accesses AWS credentials from environment variables and transmits them to an external, attacker-controlled server. This is a direct credential exfiltration technique, not related to any legitimate password hashing functionality.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: A password hashing library should never access cloud provider credentials or perform unsolicited network requests, especially to untrusted domains. Such behavior is entirely outside the scope of expected library operations.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate code in a password hashing library may read configuration from environment variables, but would never transmit secrets or credentials to third-party endpoints. Any network activity should be opt-in, documented, and never involve exfiltration of sensitive data.
key_indicators: Accessing AWS_ACCESS_KEY and AWS_SECRET_KEY in a password hashing class
Use of environment variables for credential exfiltration
Network activity triggered by class instantiation

execution_context.trigger: import-time (when the package is imported or executed)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: Upon import, the package reads all environment variables (including AWS credentials if present) and sends them to a remote Heroku endpoint controlled by the attacker. This occurs automatically, without user interaction.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code is designed to execute at import-time, harvesting all environment variables and exfiltrating them to an external server. This is a hallmark of supply chain attacks and is not part of any legitimate context management functionality.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: A context management library should not access or transmit environment variables, especially secrets, to external servers. Import-time network requests are highly abnormal and dangerous.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate telemetry might send anonymized, non-sensitive usage data, but never secrets or credentials. Any such telemetry would be opt-in and clearly documented.

detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for packages that access environment variables and make network requests at import or constructor time. Use static analysis to detect hardcoded URLs (e.g., anti-theft-web.herokuapp.com) and suspicious use of environment variable access in core files. Employ dynamic analysis to observe runtime exfiltration behavior. Flag any code that sends environment variables or credentials to external, non-affiliated domains. Monitor for unexpected changes in package metadata, such as new authors or maintainers, and for outbound network activity during package installation or import.
